Painful Dentures: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment Options

Understanding why dentures may cause discomfort, how to recognise the signs, and what professional treatment options may help improve comfort and stability.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation020 71833573

Dentures are commonly used to replace missing teeth and restore oral function, helping patients eat, speak, and smile with greater confidence. For many people, dentures provide a practical and effective solution for tooth loss, particularly when multiple teeth are missing.

However, some denture wearers experience discomfort or soreness in the gums, particularly over time. Pain may occur when dentures do not fit correctly, when the shape of the jawbone changes, or when the denture materials begin to wear. This discomfort can make chewing and speaking more difficult, and may significantly affect a patient's quality of life.

Professional dental assessment can help determine the cause of denture-related pain and identify the most appropriate treatment options. In some cases, adjustments or relining may resolve the issue, while other patients may benefit from exploring implant-supported alternatives that provide additional stability and support.

Why Dentures Can Become Painful

Dentures rely on the gums and underlying jawbone for support and stability. Unlike natural teeth, which are anchored within the bone by their roots, conventional dentures sit on top of the gum tissue and are held in place by suction, adhesive, or the shape of the jaw ridge.

Over time, the shape of the jawbone can change — a natural process known as bone resorption, which commonly occurs after teeth are lost. As the ridge of bone beneath the denture gradually reduces in height and width, the denture may begin to fit less precisely, creating areas of pressure or friction against the gum tissue.

Pressure from poorly fitting dentures may irritate the gums, causing soreness, inflammation, or ulceration. The denture materials themselves may also wear over time, affecting how the denture distributes biting forces across the gum tissue.

The cause of denture pain varies between individuals and depends on factors such as the age and condition of the denture, the health of the underlying bone and gum tissue, and how well the denture was originally fitted. A professional assessment is recommended to identify the specific cause.

Common Causes of Painful Dentures

Several factors may contribute to denture discomfort. In many cases, more than one factor is involved, and a clinical examination is needed to identify the specific cause or causes.

Poorly Fitting Dentures

Dentures that do not fit precisely against the gum tissue can create uneven pressure, leading to sore spots, irritation, and discomfort. Fit issues may be present from the outset or develop over time as the jaw changes shape.

Jawbone Shrinkage After Tooth Loss

Following tooth extraction, the jawbone gradually resorbs over time. This natural process changes the shape of the ridge that supports the denture, causing the fit to deteriorate progressively and creating areas of increased pressure on the gum tissue.

Pressure Points on Gum Tissue

Localised areas where the denture presses more firmly against the gum can create painful pressure spots. These areas may develop sores or ulcers and can make wearing the denture uncomfortable, particularly during eating.

Changes in Gum Shape Over Time

The soft tissue of the gums may change shape due to ageing, weight fluctuations, or health conditions. These changes can affect how the denture sits against the tissue and may require the denture to be relined or replaced.

Denture Wear or Damage

Over extended periods of use, denture materials may wear down, crack, or lose their original shape. Worn denture teeth may also alter the bite relationship, placing uneven forces on the gum tissue and contributing to discomfort.

Oral Health Conditions

Underlying oral health issues such as fungal infections, dry mouth, or gum disease may contribute to denture-related discomfort. These conditions can increase sensitivity of the oral tissues and make wearing dentures more painful.

Signs and Symptoms of Denture Discomfort

The signs of denture-related discomfort may develop gradually or appear suddenly. Symptoms may vary depending on denture fit, oral health, and individual sensitivity. Common signs that dentures may require professional attention include:

Sore, inflamed, or tender gums beneath the denture
Pain or discomfort when chewing or biting down on food
Localised pressure spots or ulcers under the denture
Difficulty wearing dentures comfortably for extended periods
Redness, irritation, or swelling of the oral tissues
A feeling that the denture moves or rocks when eating
Difficulty eating certain foods due to pain or instability
Changes in speech clarity when wearing the denture

If any of these symptoms are present, professional dental assessment is recommended to determine the cause and discuss available treatment options.

Potential Effects on Oral Function

Painful dentures can affect several aspects of daily life beyond the immediate discomfort. When dentures cause pain, patients may modify their eating habits, avoid certain foods, or reduce the time they wear their dentures — each of which can have wider implications for oral health and wellbeing.

Chewing efficiency is often one of the first areas affected. Patients may find it difficult to chew harder or tougher foods, leading to a restricted diet that may lack important nutrients. Over time, this can affect general health and energy levels.

Speech clarity may also be affected if the denture moves or feels unstable. Some patients report difficulty pronouncing certain words clearly, which can affect confidence in social and professional settings.

Overall oral comfort is reduced when dentures cause pain, and many patients find themselves removing their dentures more frequently to relieve discomfort. This can further affect eating, speaking, and self-confidence. Addressing the underlying cause of the pain is important for restoring function and comfort.

Treatment Options to Improve Denture Comfort

Treatment for painful dentures depends on the clinical findings and the specific cause of the discomfort. A thorough assessment is essential before determining the most appropriate approach. Options vary depending on the denture condition and the health of the underlying bone and soft tissue.

Denture Adjustment to Relieve Pressure Areas

If specific pressure spots are causing discomfort, careful adjustment of the denture base may help relieve the areas of concentrated pressure. This is often a straightforward process that can be carried out during a clinical appointment and may help improve comfort relatively quickly.

Denture Relining to Improve Fit

Where the jawbone or gum tissue has changed shape, relining the denture may help restore a more accurate fit against the tissue. This involves adding new material to the fitting surface of the denture so that it sits more comfortably and distributes pressure more evenly.

Replacement of Worn Dentures

When dentures have worn significantly or no longer provide adequate support and comfort, replacement with a new set of dentures may be recommended. New dentures can be designed to fit the current shape of the jaw and provide improved function and comfort.

Implant-Retained Dentures for Improved Support

For patients who experience ongoing discomfort with conventional dentures, implant-retained dentures may offer an alternative approach. By anchoring the denture to dental implants placed within the jawbone, movement and pressure on the gums may be significantly reduced, which may help improve comfort and stability.

When Implant-Supported Dentures May Be Considered

Dental implants can provide additional support for dentures by anchoring them directly to the jawbone. This reduces the reliance on gum tissue and suction for retention, and may help address many of the issues that cause denture-related discomfort.

Implant-retained dentures may reduce movement and rocking during eating and speaking, which in turn may decrease friction and pressure on the gums. Patients who have experienced ongoing difficulty with conventional dentures may find that implant-supported options provide a more comfortable and stable alternative.

Suitability for implant-supported dentures depends on several factors, including the health and volume of the jawbone, overall health status, and individual clinical circumstances. A thorough assessment involving dental imaging and clinical examination is required to determine whether implant treatment is appropriate.

Other implant-supported options such as All-on-4 dental implants or a full arch implant bridge may also be considered depending on the patient's needs and clinical presentation. Each approach offers different levels of support and retention, and the most appropriate option is determined through individual assessment.

Importance of Professional Assessment

Denture discomfort should be evaluated by a dental professional who can examine the denture fit, assess the health of the gum tissue and underlying bone, and determine whether the current dentures can be adjusted or whether alternative options should be considered.

Clinical examination may involve assessing the condition of the oral tissues, checking the denture for wear or damage, and evaluating how well the denture fits against the gum ridge. Where implant treatment is being considered, dental imaging may be required to assess bone volume and quality.

Treatment planning varies depending on individual needs, and a personalised approach ensures that the most appropriate solution is recommended for each patient. Whether the treatment involves denture adjustment, relining, replacement, or an implant-supported approach, clinical assessment is the essential first step.

Assessment and treatment planning for denture discomfort and stability concerns are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate restorative options.
